newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Inflation deters Bank/Portugal rate cut - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Inflation deters Bank/Portugal rate cut - analysts.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal left its key draining rate unchanged on Monday, defying market predictions of a cut, because of unease over inflation and last week's relative currency instability, analysts said.

They had widely forecast the Bank would lower the rate at which it absorbs excess market funds as much as 30 basis points to 6.50 percent from the start of the new commercial bank reserve period on Tuesday.

"I was expecting a cut, but I think the decision (to hold) had something to do with the exchange instability last week. The Bank is now waiting for the inflation (for October)," said Isabel Cabral of Fincor.
Analysts said uncertainty over the outcome of public sector wage talks could also have influenced the Bank's decision.

Public sector unions have rejected a 2.38 percent offer but the government says it cannot afford to be more generous without jeorpardising Portugal's chances of qualifying for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Higher salaries could pressure inflation as well as complicate the task of reducing the budget deficit, it says.
"The principal motive that I see (for the Bank's stance) is that it is waiting for the wage talks," said Finantia's Joao Morais.
The analyst said that room for a cut had existed for some time but the Bank was apparently concerned about inflation and its future trend, which would depend on the salary talks.

In its latest economic report, the Bank warned on Monday that the government would not be able to meet its ambitious target of an average inflation rate of 2.25-2.50 percent next year unless it kept a tight lid on wage rises.

It predicted that the 12-month moving average would stand at 3.25 percent at the end of 1996, adding that it would be difficult to make further progress on reducing the rate until after the first quarter of 1997.
"Progress towards disinflation is going to have to be particularly rapid in the last nine months of the year," it added.
